papers.title_in_file: A benchmarking procedure for quantum networks
papers.version_note: arXiv:2103.01165v1, dated March 2, 2021; the text layer holds the paper twice (plain and layout extraction); the first copy was read and the second used only to check quotes.
papers.what_it_is: A theory-and-simulation paper that adapts randomized benchmarking to estimate the fidelity of quantum network links (2-node and multi-node protocols), with a teleportation lemma, Netsquid simulations and a sampling-cost argument.

existing.note: The paper adds a second assumption beside Markovianity: gate-independent noise for local gates, which it calls a technical assumption that can be removed at a cost in mathematical complexity. The noise on state preparation, measurement and gates is also assumed to depend only on the node.
existing.value: The authors state that network benchmarking is not device independent and that its fidelity estimate rests on assumptions essentially the same as those of standard randomized benchmarking: the central one is Markovianity (the link noise is always the same quantum channel, independent of its history, and node noise depends only on the node), and they also assume a gate-independent noise model for local gates, a technical assumption they say can be removed at the cost of a considerable increase in mathematical complexity.
quotes: Network benchmarking is not a device independent protocol
These assumptions are essentially the same as those of standard randomized benchmarking
The central assumption we make is that of Markovianity: we will assume that the noise in the network link is always modeled by the same quantum channel, independent of the history of its use.
have noise models that only depend on the node A (and not on external variables like time, history, etc..)
We will also assume that the quantum gates UA has a so-called gate-independent noise model.
It can be removed at the cost of a considerable increase in mathematical complexity
existing.certainty_reason: Section III states the protocol's assumptions as the paper's own scope.

existing.note: The paper also gives the outcome of the argument: through the Cramer-Rao bound the estimator variance is of order r (the infidelity), which gives additive but not relative accuracy, and it says additive accuracy is enough in the near term.
existing.value: The authors argue, with an argument they say is not strictly rigorous because it makes standard statistical assumptions such as normality, that multiplicative accuracy cannot be achieved for fidelity estimation when the number of state transmissions is the cost metric; bounding the Fisher information per unit of sampling cost, they conclude through the Cramer-Rao bound that the variance of the infidelity estimator is of order r, which provides additive, but not relative, estimation accuracy.
quotes: we can not achieve 'multiplicative accuracy' for the estimation of fidelity when taking the number of state transmissions as a cost metric
The argument below is not strictly rigorous as we will be making standard statistical assumptions such as normality of distributions
This implies through the Cramer-Rao bound that
providing additive, but not relative, estimation accuracy
existing.certainty_reason: A heuristic argument the authors call not strictly rigorous.
The Abstract and Section I define the protocol.

existing.note: The paper gives the end point and the uncertainties: 0.899 ± 0.04 at two nodes to 0.56 ± 0.02 at six nodes, from 40 random sequences per bounce number m from 1 to 9.
existing.value: The authors report that in a Netsquid simulation of n nodes in a linear configuration, with n from 2 to 6 and links modeled by teleportation, run for 40 random sequences for each number of bounces m from 1 to 9, the network fidelity decreases from 0.899 ± 0.04 at two nodes to 0.56 ± 0.02 at six nodes (95% Studentized confidence interval from the fit), and that empirically it decays exponentially with the number of nodes.
quotes: we performed multi-node network benchmark on n nodes in a linear configuration, where n ranges between 2 and 6
by running the n-node network benchmarking protocol for 40 random sequences for each number of bounces m (ranging from 1 to 9)
the network fidelity decreases from 0.899 ± 0.04 at two nodes (line markers), to 0.56 ± 0.02 at six nodes (hexagon markers, 95% Studentized confidence interval from the fit)
We note that empirically the network fidelity decays exponentially with the number of nodes
existing.certainty_reason: A simulation result from one study.
existing.reader_inference: The two-node value is printed as 0.899 ± 0.004 in Section V.A and as 0.899 ± 0.04 in Section V.B; one of the two is likely a typo.

assertions.value: The authors quantify the quality of a network link by the average fidelity of the quantum channel modeling it, an integral taken uniformly over all pure quantum states, and use the closely related depolarizing fidelity, which they say shows up more naturally in the calculations.
quotes: One of the most common ways of quantifying this approximation is the average fidelity F (Λ) of a quantum channel Λ
where the integral is taken uniformly over all pure quantum states
which we call the depolarizing fidelity f (Λ)
but it will show up more naturally in the calculations below
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II.B defines the quantities the results are stated in.

assertions.value: The authors model network nodes with three functionalities from the quantum internet stages framework: storing quantum states in memory (stage 4), performing quantum operations on stored states (stage 5), and transmitting quantum states between nodes (stage 3), the last being the ability the protocol predominantly tests.
quotes: (1) The ability to store quantum states in memory (stage 4 in [5]).
(2) The ability to perform quantum operations on stored quantum states (stage 5 in [5]).
(3) The ability to transmit quantum states from a node A to a node B (stage 3 in [5]).
It is this ability that is predominantly tested by network benchmarking.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II.A states the network model.

assertions.value: The authors require the procedure to be efficient (light on link uses and independent of link capacity) and robust to state preparation and measurement errors, and state that independence from local operation noise is not possible; they call SPAM robustness alone a reasonable compromise because gate fidelities are typically much higher than SPAM fidelities.
quotes: The first property is efficiency: we demand that the estimation procedure is light on resource use
The second property is resistance to state preparation and measurement errors.
Ideally we would also like to demand independence of noise in quantum operations performed locally, but this is not possible.
demanding only SPAM-robustness is a reasonable compromise
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III states what the protocol does and does not guarantee.

assertions.value: The authors define the 2-node protocol as m bounces of a random gate at A, transmission to B, a random gate at B and transmission back, with gates drawn from a set that must be at least a unitary 2-design (the multi-qubit Clifford group is a common choice), followed by an inverting gate with a random ending gate; the averaged outcomes are fitted to a single exponential A f to the power m, where A depends on SPAM errors and f only on local gate noise and the link channels.
quotes: By sufficiently large we mean that the set must be at least a unitary 2-design.
A com- mon choice for such a set is the multi-qubit Clifford group C [25], which is also appropriate here.
the output data {bm}m∈M can be fitted to a single exponential
where A depends on state preparation and measurement (SPAM) errors and f only depends on the noise incurred by the application of local gates and the channels
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III.A and Algorithm 1 define the protocol.
assertions.reader_inference: The second quote keeps the text layer's line-break hyphen in 'com- mon' as printed.

assertions.value: The authors argue that, under gate-independent local noise and using that the gate set is a 2-design (so each twirl is a depolarizing channel), the fitted network link fidelity is the product of the depolarizing fidelities of the two link channels each composed with local gate noise, and state that in practice it is dominated by the link channels because local gates have high fidelity relative to the links.
assertions.anchor: Section III.A and Section IV, eqs. (9)-(12), pp.4-5
quotes: the network link fidelity f can be written as f = f (ΛA→BΛA)f (ΛB→AΛB), with f (Λ) the depolarizing fidelity
Now we can use the fact that G is a 2-design to conclude that this twirl operator
We will for this section assume that the network obeys the property of gate-independent noise.
In practice the local gates will have high fidelity relative to the communication links
assertions.certainty_reason: A derivation the paper presents as an argument adapted from randomized benchmarking; the gate-independence condition is quoted.

assertions.value: The authors state that the multi-node protocol, sending a state from the first to the last node and back with a random gate at each node, outputs (under gate-independent local noise) the product of the depolarizing fidelities of all intermediate links up to local noise, which they call the network path fidelity and present as a quantum version of the classical ping command.
quotes: In other words the output of the multi-node network benchmarking protocol is given by the product of the depolarizing fidelities of all intermediate communication links (up to local noise channels).
We will refer to f as the network path fidelity
This provides a quantum version of the classical 'ping' command
assertions.certainty_reason: Said to follow by an argument identical to the 2-node case.

assertions.value: The paper proves (Lemma 1) that if two link channels are implemented by teleportation using resource states ρAB and ρBA and the local operations in the teleportation are noiseless, then the two channels have equal average fidelity; the proof uses that the entanglement fidelity of a teleportation channel equals the singlet fraction of its resource state, which is invariant under interchange of A and B.
quotes: Lemma 1. Let ΛA→B be the quantum channel implemented by teleportation using a state ρAB as a resource, and let ΛB→A be the quantum channel implemented by teleportation using a state ρBA as a resource.
If the local operations used in the teleportation process are noiseless, then F (ΛA→B) = F (ΛB→A).
Now noting that the singlet fraction is invariant under the interchange of A and B
assertions.certainty_reason: Lemma 1 is stated with its condition and proved in Section IV.A.

assertions.value: The authors state that for teleportation-implemented links the network fidelity measured by the 2-node protocol can be connected directly to the average fidelity of the links A to B and B to A, assuming negligible contributions from local noise.
quotes: In this case we can thus connect the network fidelity f , as measured by the 2-node protocol, to the average fidelity of the network links A → B and B → A (assuming negligible contributions from local noise).
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from Lemma 1 and eq. (2), with the negligible-local-noise condition quoted.

assertions.value: The authors state that their Netsquid simulations use the single-qubit Clifford group as local gate set and an abstracted, simplified noise model inspired by NV-centre networks, modeling T1 and T2 noise on node qubits and teleportation-like link channels and omitting other imperfections, and that the intent is not a detailed physical simulation (waiting times and non-deterministic entanglement creation are not taken into account).
quotes: For both these simulations we choose the local gate set to be the single qubit Clifford group C1.
a noise model that is an abstracted and simplified version of the noise present in networks based on NV-centres [31]
We however emphasize that our intent is not to produce a detailed physical simulation of networks of this form
account e.g. waiting times and non-deterministic entanglement creation)
and omit other imperfections
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V states the simulation's scope.

assertions.value: The authors report that in a Netsquid simulation of 2-node network benchmarking with teleportation links using a noisy entangled state of bright state population α = 0.95, T2 = 12ms dephasing on memory qubits and 39μs native operations, run for 40 random sequences per bounce number m from 1 to 20 with Gaussian noise added for 4000 measurements per sequence, the exponential fit gives f = 0.899 ± 0.004 (95% Studentized confidence interval), which they say is in line with a fidelity dominated by the teleportation quality.
quotes: For our simulation we choose a bright state population of α = 0.95
processors being T2 = 12ms
operations on these memory qubits takes 39μs
The data in fig. 2 is generated by running the 2-node network benchmarking protocol for 40 random sequences for each number of bounces m (ranging from 1 to 20).
We add Gaussian noise to the data to simulate shot noise for 4000 measurements per random sequence.
From the exponential decay fit we obtain f = 0.899 ± 0.004 (95% Studentized confidence interval from the fit) which is in line with a fidelity dominated by the quality of the teleportation procedure.
assertions.certainty_reason: A simulation result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors note that the noise model of their simulation is not gate-independent, because some single-qubit Clifford gates must be compiled out of native operations.
quotes: We note that since some of the gates in the single qubit Clifford group must be compiled out of native operations this is not a gate-independent noise model.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its simulation setup.
assertions.reader_inference: So the simulation tests the protocol outside the gate-independence assumption used in the Section IV derivation.

assertions.value: The authors state that the exponential decay with node count points to a potential use of network benchmarking as a network discovery tool, giving heuristic estimates of upper limits on how far quantum information can travel through a network before degrading.
quotes: This points to a potential use of network benchmarking as a network discovery tool
to give heuristic estimates of upper limits on the distance quantum information can travel through a network before degrading
assertions.certainty_reason: A suggestion without evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that in network benchmarking the cost of transmitting a qubit dominates the cost of a sample, so a sequence of m bounces is approximately m times as expensive as one bounce, and accuracy should be measured against the number of bounces rather than the number of measurements as in standard randomized benchmarking analyses.
quotes: as the cost of transmitting a qubit over a long distance will be the dominant factor in the cost of a sample
will be approximately m times as expensive as sampling a sequence containing only one bounce
it is more appropriate to estimate accuracy of the fidelity estimate produced by algorithm 1 as a function of the number of bounces
assertions.certainty_reason: The cost model Section VI adopts for its analysis.

assertions.value: The authors state that network fidelities in the immediate future are expected to be reasonably low, in the 90 to 99% regime, so additive rather than multiplicative accuracy is enough for practical purposes, and that the simulations show good statistical accuracy for reasonable resource use.
quotes: in the immediate future network fidelities are expected to be reasonably low (in the 90∼99% regime), so additive, and not multiplicative, accuracy is enough for practical purposes
network benchmarking achieves good statistical accuracy for a reasonable resource use in practice
assertions.certainty_reason: An expectation stated without evidence.

assertions.value: The authors argue that standard randomized benchmarking's multiplicative precision (estimator variance of order r squared) depends critically on the assumption that sampling cost is independent of sequence length, and that their argument applies equally to standard randomized benchmarking if the number of gates implemented is taken as the cost.
quotes: We will argue here that this behavior is critically dependent on the assumption that the cost of obtaining samples from a given gate sequence in a (network) benchmarking experiment is independent of the sequence length.
the argument below works just as well for standard randomized benchmarking if one takes the number of gates implemented as a cost function
assertions.certainty_reason: Part of the same not strictly rigorous argument.
assertions.reader_inference: The 'order r squared' restates the text layer's flattened 'O(r2)' in words; it is not inside the quotes.

assertions.value: The authors state that the assumptions of their analysis can be relaxed significantly by adapting more modern treatments of randomized benchmarking to network benchmarking, but they do not pursue this.
quotes: the assumptions we make can be relaxed significantly by adapting the more modern treatments of randomized benchmarking
but we will not pursue this here
assertions.certainty_reason: Rests on cited work; not done in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that a natural next step is to implement network benchmarking in real quantum networks, which are in development, and on the theory side to investigate it as a tool for network discovery and as a subroutine in online routing algorithms.
quotes: A natural next step would be to implement the network benchmarking protocol in real quantum networks, which are currently in development.
integrating it as a subroutine in online routing algorithms for quantum networks
assertions.certainty_reason: The conclusion states the protocol has not yet been run on a real network.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that they presented a robust and efficient protocol in two-node and multi-node versions, argued that under some assumptions it outputs a quantity related to the average fidelity of the link channels, showed that for noisy teleportation the network fidelity can be exactly related to the average fidelity, and saw in simulation that it works well in realistic environments.
quotes: arguing that under some assumptions they output a quantity related tot the average fidelity of the quantum channels modeling the network links
namely noisy quantum teleportation, the network fidelity can be exactly related to the average fidelity of the link
From these simulations we saw that network benchmarking works well in realistic environments.
assertions.certainty_reason: Summary of mixed theoretical and simulated results.

papers.title_in_file: Generative Quantum Data Embeddings for Supervised Learning
papers.version_note: arXiv:2605.30866v1, 29 May 2026; the text layer holds the paper twice (plain and layout extraction); the first copy was read and the second used only to check quotes.
papers.what_it_is: A QML methods paper that searches quantum data-embedding circuits with an energy-based GPT generator (EGAS), refines them with a learnable bias, evaluates them with a quantum kernel SVM on eight tabular datasets, and bounds the attainable empirical risk of an embedding family by the input-space 1-Wasserstein distance.

existing.note: The same sentence adds that deployment also needs a systematic analysis of the depth-noise trade-off; Appendix A shows all results come from noiseless analytic simulation (shots=None), which bounds the claim further.
existing.value: The authors state that deployment on near-term quantum hardware will require search spaces tailored to hardware-native gate sets and connectivity constraints, together with a systematic analysis of how the trade-off between circuit depth and noise affects classification performance; all reported results come from PennyLane simulation with analytic probabilities, so that differences between embeddings are not affected by finite-shot noise.
existing.anchor: Section V Conclusion (future work); Appendix A, p.9
quotes: Finally, deployment on near-term quantum hardware will require search spaces tailored to hardware-native gate sets and connectivity constraints
together with a systematic analysis of how the trade-off between circuit depth and noise affects classification performance
Quantum simulation is carried out with PennyLane's lightning.qubit backend using analytic probabilities (shots=None)
so that the reported differences between embeddings are not affected by finite-shot measurement noise
existing.certainty_reason: The conclusion and Appendix A state the hardware gap and the simulation setting.
An empirical result from one study.
existing.reader_inference: The Fig. 7 table is consistent: on EGSSD every quantum embedding scores the same mean accuracy as NQE and ZZ, so 'matches' carries that dataset.

existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

existing.note: The paper states the conditions of the bound (balanced class priors, Helstrom measurement, an embedding family of fixed sequence length built from a fixed subcircuit pool), says it may be loose, and proves it in Appendix B; the stored value had none of these.
existing.value: The authors derive, for an embedding family generated with a fixed sequence length and a fixed subcircuit pool and assuming balanced class priors, a lower bound on the empirical risk attainable by any embedding in the family under the Helstrom measurement, in terms of a family-level Lipschitz constant times the 1-Wasserstein distance between the empirical class-conditional input distributions (proof in Appendix B); they state the bound may be loose, and that it gives an a priori diagnostic of datasets where large architecture-dependent gains from embedding optimization are unlikely.
existing.anchor: Section II.B, eqs. (5)-(8); Appendix B; Abstract, pp.3-8
quotes: Let F denote the family of embedding structures generated under this fixed sequence length and fixed subcircuit pool.
By definition, this minimum transport cost is precisely the 1-Wasserstein distance
Assuming balanced class priors, combining Eq. (1) with Eq. (7) gives a lower bound on the empirical risk attainable by any embedding Φ ∈ F
denotes the minimum empirical risk achievable over the embedding family when the Helstrom measurement is used
The bound may be loose because of the relaxation
This analysis provides an a priori diagnostic for identifying datasets in which large architecture-dependent gains are unlikely within a fixed embedding family.
existing.certainty_reason: The bound's own formula is lost in the text layer (math italic letters print as replacement characters), so the statement cannot be quoted; its conditions are quoted.
existing.reader_inference: The text layer loses the bound's symbols; the page image (p.3, eqs. (6)-(8)) shows the bound as R-hat-star(X, y; F) at least 1/2 minus (1/2) kappa_F W1(P-hat-plus(x), P-hat-minus(x)), with kappa_F = D Delta_F / 2, D the sequence length and Delta_F the family-level maximal spectral spread of the gate generators.

assertions.value: The authors state that most QML studies adopt a fixed embedding chosen a priori, that hand-designed feature maps such as the ZZ feature map are typically data-agnostic, and that even NQE, which optimizes a classical preprocessing network, remains confined to the transformations expressible by the chosen circuit ansatz.
quotes: most QML studies adopt a fixed mapping scheme chosen a priori, such as amplitude or angle encoding
such hand-designed feature maps are typically data-agnostic
the quantum embedding remains confined to the family of transformations expressible by the chosen ansatz
assertions.certainty_reason: Motivating claims in the introduction.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing prior work, that amplitude encoding can incur nontrivial state-preparation overhead as data dimension grows, while simple angle encoding may yield product states that admit efficient classical simulation.
quotes: amplitude encoding can incur nontrivial state-preparation overhead as
the data dimension grows, while simple angle encoding may yield product states and therefore admit efficient classical simulation [7]
assertions.certainty_reason: Attributed to cited work.

assertions.value: The authors state that evolutionary circuit search may sample candidates inefficiently and need extensive evaluations, and that reinforcement-learning circuit construction suffers from high-variance gradients in data-driven settings and requires intermediate measurements after each sub-circuit attachment.
quotes: it may sample candidates inefficiently and thus requires extensive evaluations
it suffers from a high-variance gradient issue in data-driven settings
requires intermediate measurements after each elemental sub-circuit attachment
assertions.certainty_reason: Claims about prior methods without evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the trace distance between the prior-weighted class states determines the minimum achievable error probability, so the empirical risk of any measurement or classifier is bounded below by one half minus that trace distance, with equality for the Helstrom measurement, and that subsequent quantum processing cannot increase it because trace distance is contractive under CPTP maps.
quotes: which determines the minimum achievable error probability for distinguishing the two hypotheses
with equality achieved by the Helstrom measurement [15]
This distinguishability cannot be increased by subsequent quantum processing because trace distance is contractive under completely positive trace-preserving maps
assertions.certainty_reason: Standard results attributed to cited work.

assertions.value: The authors use pairwise fidelity between embedded pure states as a tractable surrogate for trace-distance separability, because trace distance is costly to compute on near-term devices while overlaps can be estimated more cheaply (for example by a swap test); the pairwise loss rewards large overlaps for same-class pairs and small overlaps for cross-class pairs, but they state it does not guarantee that the class mixtures can be made arbitrarily distinguishable.
quotes: computing it is costly on near-term quantum devices [43]
as a tractable surrogate for trace-distancebased separability
overlaps between pure states can be estimated at substantially lower cost, for example via a swap test [44]
Minimizing l
promotes large overlaps for same-class pairs and small overlaps for cross-class pairs
it does not guarantee that the class-conditional mixtures can be made arbitrarily distinguishable
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II.A defines the objective the method optimizes.

assertions.value: The authors define EGAS as representing an embedding circuit as a fixed-length sequence of depth-one subcircuit tokens (gate type, qubit index, data index, parameter coefficient) generated autoregressively by a GPT, scoring each sequence by the batch-average pairwise fidelity loss as its energy, and training the GPT with a logit-matching loss toward a Boltzmann-like distribution so that lower-energy sequences get higher sampling probability, using a replay buffer.
quotes: we propose an energy-based generative architecture search (EGAS) framework
Each token is specified by a tuple
(gate type, qubit index, data index, parameter coefficient)
we assign to
an energy given by the empirical average of the pairwise fidelity loss over a batch
EGAS uses a logit-matching objective that trains the generator to approximate a Boltzmann-like distribution over the evaluated energy landscape
As a result, sequences with lower evaluated energy are assigned higher sampling probability.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III.A defines the method.

assertions.value: The authors define a post-search continuous refinement that adds a learnable bias function (initialized to zero) to each data-dependent gate angle while holding the circuit architecture, feature index and base coefficient fixed, trained with a binary cross-entropy loss on clipped pairwise fidelities.
quotes: is a parameterized bias function that provides a learnable additive offset
During refinement, the circuit architecture, selected feature index
are held fixed; only the bias-function parameters
The bias function is initialized as
are optimized using a binary cross-entropy loss over a batch
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III.B defines the refinement step.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the Phishing Website dataset continuous bias refinement reduced the surrogate energy for all 20 selected candidate circuits (the ten lowest- and ten highest-energy unique EGAS outputs, each refined ten times), with modest stable reductions for the low-energy group and larger, more variable reductions for several high-energy candidates.
quotes: Figure 3 reports this quantity for the Phishing Website (PW) [50] dataset over the 20 selected candidate circuits.
continuous parameter refinement reduces the surrogate energy for all selected candidate structures
Each candidate embedding was refined ten times.
The reductions are generally modest and stable for the initially low-energy
candidates exhibit larger reductions, often accompanied by larger variability across repeated runs
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that across eight datasets continuous refinement frequently reduces the surrogate energy, with a strongly dataset-dependent magnitude and no universal ordering between the low- and high-energy groups, and that on DB and WC the mean reduction is close to zero or slightly negative.
quotes: The cross-dataset results show that continuous refinement frequently reduces the surrogate energy, while the magnitude and group-wise pattern of the reduction remain strongly dataset-dependent.
does not exhibit a universal ordering
In datasets such as DB and WC, the mean reduction is close to zero or slightly negative.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors evaluate embeddings by a quantum kernel SVM over ten train-test splits, each of 400 training and 50 test samples, against a classical linear SVM on standardized features, scoring each split as a win, tie or loss and reporting for each EGAS group the candidate with the most wins.
quotes: each embedding is evaluated over ten train-test splits
The classical baseline is a linear SVM trained on the standardized classical input features.
producing a win, tie, or loss
we report the embedding that achieves the largest number of wins against the classical baseline across the ten train-test splits
consisting of 400 training samples and 50 test samples
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV.B and Appendix A state the evaluation protocol.
assertions.reader_inference: Reporting the best-of-ten candidate per group is a selection step; the win counts of the starred models are best cases within each group.

assertions.value: The authors report that the selected representative of the refined low-energy group most frequently achieves the strongest performance, that the data-agnostic ZZ feature map is often among the weakest models, and that NQE generally sits in between, improving over ZZ in many cases without consistently matching the best EGAS-derived architectures.
quotes: (Bias) group most frequently achieves the strongest performance
The dataagnostic ZZ feature map is often among the weakest models,
it improves over ZZ in many cases but does not consistently match the best EGAS-derived architectures
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that refinement cannot compensate for every unfavorable architecture: on WDGV1 the selected refined high-energy embedding remains weak after refinement, and they conclude refinement complements rather than substitutes for choosing a suitable circuit structure.
quotes: the results show that refinement cannot compensate for every unfavorable architecture
embedding remains weak even after refinement
continuous parameter refinement should be viewed as a complementary step to architecture search, rather than as a substitute for selecting an appropriate circuit structure
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that on WQ, MGT and EGSSD the winning summary is weak: on WQ no selected EGAS embedding shows a clear advantage over the classical baseline and ties dominate, on MGT the selected embeddings lose to the classical baseline on several splits, and on EGSSD all models show nearly identical win-tie-loss patterns.
quotes: For WQ, none of the selected EGAS-derived embeddings shows a clear advantage over the classical baseline
For MGT, the selected EGAS-derived embeddings lose to the classical baseline on several splits
For EGSSD, all evaluated models exhibit nearly identical win-tie-loss patterns
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that WQ, MGT and EGSSD have markedly smaller interquartile ranges of mean QKSVM accuracy across embeddings and are also the three datasets with the smallest empirical 1-Wasserstein distances between class-conditional inputs (3.0112, 3.3036 and 3.5619, against 4.3543 to 13.9108 for the others), which they call consistent with the Wasserstein-based bound.
assertions.anchor: Section IV.B, Fig. 6, Table I, p.8
quotes: By contrast, WQ, MGT, and EGSSD have markedly smaller IQR values.
The three datasets with the smallest Wasserstein distances are WQ, MGT, and EGSSD, which are also the datasets with weak variation in QKSVM accuracy across the evaluated embeddings
This agreement is consistent with the Wasserstein-based discussion in Section II B

assertions.value: The authors report in Appendix C a table of mean and standard deviation of test accuracy over ten train-test splits for the classical linear SVM, a classical RBF SVM, the ZZ and NQE baselines and every EGAS-derived embedding on all eight datasets; on EGSSD the classical linear SVM scores 0.586 ± 0.097, the RBF SVM 0.612 ± 0.084, and every quantum embedding row 0.620 ± 0.071.
quotes: Each cell reports the mean and standard deviation of the test accuracy over ten independent train-test splits.
rows correspond to the classical linear SVM baseline, the classical RBF SVM, the vanilla ZZ feature map, the NQE-augmented ZZ feature map
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Reading the table's last column (EGSSD) across all rows shows every quantum embedding at 0.620 ± 0.071, which supports the paper's insensitivity finding for EGSSD.

assertions.value: The authors report a simulation in which one class is held fixed and the other translated: the trace distance between class states first increases with the input 1-Wasserstein distance and then saturates near its maximum, and a double-layer ZZ feature map saturates at smaller Wasserstein distances than a single-layer one.

assertions.value: The authors define SPSB (Simultaneous Perturbation for Stochastic Backpropagation) as estimating the Jacobian of a quantum or hybrid layer from one pair of evaluations at a random plus-or-minus-one perturbation, as the outer product of the output difference with the element-wise inverse of the perturbation divided by twice the shift, and using that Jacobian in reverse-mode automatic differentiation via the chain rule; it is implemented in PennyLane, with versions for TensorFlow-Quantum and qujax.
quotes: We refer to our method as Simultaneous Perturbation for Stochastic Backpropagation (SPSB).
where we denote by ⊗ the outer product, and by ∆ −1 the element-wise inverse of ∆
Now that we have an estimation of the Jacobian matrix, we can use SPSA-like gradients for Automatic Differentiation as described in Section 2.1.
This method, which we refer to as SPSB, was implemented in PennyLane
Furthermore, we provide SPSB implementations for TensorFlow-Quantum [4] and qujax [7].

assertions.value: The authors conclude that SPSB significantly improves training speed of hybrid models through its favourable scaling over the parameter shift rule, is well adapted to large batches and circuits with many parameters, and expect that for large batches its extra gradient noise may help escape zero-gradient regions such as barren plateaus.
quotes: significantly improves the speed of training quantum hybrid models due to its favourable scaling over the parameter shift rule
We show that this algorithm is well-adapted to cope with large batches of data and with circuits with large parameter numbers

For large batch sizes, we expect our method to help avoid local minima due to the introduction of additional statistical noise on the gradients which can help escape regions in the parameter landscape with zero-gradients, i.e. barren plateaus.
